paraphrase: At the beginning knowledge became twofold according to the difference of those qualified (adhikārin), as higher and lower. The knowledge that reveals Śiva, called Śiva-knowledge (śivajñāna), is remembered as the higher; the lower knowledge, beginning with the Veda, makes known the bound soul and its bonds (paśu, pāśa). As the eyes of a man and of a cat differ at night, so this knowledge differs as higher and lower.

paraphrase: Within these is contained all verbal lore; among them the Mantra-tantra issued from Sadāśiva's faces as Siddhānta, Gāruḍa, Vāma, Bhūta tantra and Bhairava (v. 21 names the upper, eastern, northern and southern faces in order; v. 26 assigns the Bhūta tantras to Sadyojāta). The knowledge from the upper Īśāna face, beginning with the Kāmika, was told in ten and eighteen divisions by Śiva- and Rudra-transmitters; the Gāruḍa came from the eastern face; the Vāma from the Vāma face, twenty-four in number beginning with the Nayasūtra; the Bhūta tantra, twenty in number beginning with 'Kaula', from Sadyojāta; and the Bhairava tantra, twofold, from the southern face, told on earth in many forms by Asitāṅga and the others. (Verses 22–23 on the number of transmitters and on revelation in the ages are not paraphrased here.)

paraphrase: The descent of the Siddhānta tantras is told: ten Śiva-divisions (Kāmika, Yogaja, Cintya, Kāraṇa, Ajita, Dīpta, Sūkṣma, Sahasra, Aṃśumān, Suprabheda) and eighteen Rudra-divisions (Vijaya, Niśvāsa, Svāyambhuva, Āgneya, Vīra, Raurava, Makuṭa, Vimala, Candrajñāna, Mukhabimba, Prodgīta, Lalita, Siddha, Santāna, Śarvokta, Pārameśvara, Kiraṇa, Vātula). For each it names the being to whom it was first taught (e.g. the Kāmika to Praṇava), its extent in verses (e.g. a parārdha for the Kāmika), the chain of later recipients (Praṇava → Trikala → Hara) and its sub-divisions (upabheda); the Suprabheda has none. It concludes: these are the root divisions of the twenty-eight tantras.

paraphrase: The twenty-eight tantras are the limbs of Sadāśiva's body made of tantras and mantra-forms: the Kāmika is his two feet, Yogaja the ankles, Cintya the toes, Kāraṇa the shanks, Ajita the knees, Dīpta the thighs, Sūkṣma the private part, Sahasra the hips, Aṃśumān the back, Suprabheda the navel, Vijaya the belly, Niśvāsa the heart, Svāyambhuva the two breasts, Anala the eyes, Vīra the throat, Raurava the ears, Makuṭa the crown, Vimala the arms, Candrajñāna the chest, Bimba the face, Prodgīta the tongue, Lalita the cheeks, Siddha the forehead, Santāna the ear-ornaments, Śarvokta the sacred thread, Pārameśa the necklace, Kiraṇa the jewel ornaments and Vātula the garment; the Śivadharma is named for the tripuṇḍra mark and unguent (vv. 100–101 are partly unclear in the printed text). With their sub-divisions the Sādākhya stands embodied. This Śiva- and Rudra-tantra shines like a wish-granting gem, one and many; though the speaker is one, it is manifold through the difference of hearers.

Whatever tantra one began with, from ploughing to worship, everything is to be done by it, not from another tantra — unless something is not specifically stated there, in which case one may have it done by another tantra.

paraphrase: Worship (arcana), giving enjoyment and liberation, is twofold: for oneself (svārtha) and for others (parārtha). Worship for oneself is performed in the liṅga given by the guru at the end of initiation, or on a ground-altar (sthaṇḍila) and the like, and gives one's own desired fruit. Worship for others is performed in Śiva temples — in villages, towns, by rivers or on mountains, in the sixty-eight great holy places or elsewhere — with self-manifest, divine, bāṇa and sages' liṅgas or with liṅgas installed by men, for the increase of the king's life, health, victory and prosperity.

paraphrase: Garuḍa asks why, if Śiva's power is always present in the soul, bondage does not always end, and what 'the time' of the descent is. The Lord answers that words are used figuratively: as the cutting of bonds is spoken of, so the 'descent of power' (śaktinipāta) in the Śiva-scripture is figurative; as the sudden fall of a thing causes fear, the descent of power is said to cause fear of worldly existence. As a teacher wakes sleeping pupils with a stick, so Śiva by his power awakens those asleep in the sleep of delusion; when there is knowledge of one's own nature it is said to have 'fallen'. Its time is the equality of karma (karmaṇaḥ tulyatā).

paraphrase: Knowing their own office to be very hard to fulfil, teachers and others who seek mastery should strive for self-possession; that self-possession, which is the yogin's state, belongs to one who has conquered the senses, and conquest of the senses comes gradually through practising breath-control and the rest. Breath-control (prāṇāyāma), withdrawal (pratyāhāra), fixation (dhāraṇā), meditation (dhyāna), examination (vīkṣaṇa), recitation (japa) and absorption (samādhi) are the limbs; the possessor of the limbs, yoga itself, is the eighth.

paraphrase: Prāṇa is the air described before; its restraint is its exertion, marked by propelling, drawing in and holding, and it removes the faults of ritual. When the mind then tastes a little happiness, withdrawal is to be practised — turning back from everything. Thereby turned away from contact of senses and objects, the mind becomes fit for fixation on a place chosen at will. Thought upon that object, directed again and again, is meditation; when it becomes one continuous flow, that is called absorption. Recitation is the uttering of it, bringing the object of meditation face to face; examination (ūha) is the scrutiny arising after the object has been conceived — knowing the place, what is to be rejected and accepted there, what sustains it and what opposes it.

paraphrase: Explaining 'ten' and 'eighteen', Jayaratha quotes the Śrīkaṇṭhīya: in the upper stream knowledge is twofold, called Śiva and Rudra — Kāmaja, Yogaja, Cintya, Maukuṭa, Aṃśumat, Dīpta … (lacuna) … are the Śiva-divisions; the Rudra-divisions are Vijaya, Niḥśvāsa, Madgīta, Pārameśvara, Mukhabimba, Siddha, Santāna, Nārasiṃha, Candrāṃśu, Vīrabhadra, Āgneya, Svayambhuva, Visara, Raurava, Vimala, Kiraṇa, Lalita and Saurabheya — twenty-eight tantras issuing from the upper stream; the Śiva-division was spoken by Śivas, the Rudra-division by Rudras.
speaker: Jayaratha (quoting the Śrīkaṇṭhīya)
notes: Phase-B author read the passage in the local e-text (sources_raw/raw_etexts/AgamAH/shaivam/tantrAlokaH_viveka-vyAkhyA-sahitaH-1.md (Tantrāloka with Jayaratha's Viveka, KSTS vol. 1)); level stays 'skeleton' until Phase C/D. The quoted Śivabheda list is lacunose after 'Dīpta'.

paraphrase: Jayaratha quotes the Śrīkaṇṭhīya's sixty-four Bhairava tantras in eight groups — Bhairava, Yāmala, Mata, Maṅgala, Cakrāṣṭaka, Śikhāṣṭaka, Bahurūpa, Vāgīśa: (1) spoken by Bahurūpa: Svacchanda, Bhairava, Caṇḍa, Krodha, Unmattabhairava, Asitāṅga, Mahocchuṣma, Kapālīśa; (2) Brahmayāmala, Viṣṇuyāmala, Svacchanda, Ruru, (fifth not named in the quoted text), Ātharvaṇa, Rudra, Vetāla; (3) the Mata group, 'divisions of Caṇḍa': Rakta, Lampaṭa, Lakṣmīmata, (a fourth, 'Mata'), Cālikā, Piṅgala, Utphullaka, Viśvādya; (4) the Maṅgala group, spoken by Krodheśa: Bhairavī arising from the Picu tantra (twofold), a third, Brāhmī Kalā, Vijayā, Candrā, Maṅgalā, Sarvamaṅgalā; (5) spoken by Asitāṅga: the Mantra-, Varṇa-, Śakti-, Kalā-, Bindu-, Nāda-, Guhya- and Kha-cakras; (6) spoken by Ruru: Andhaka, Rurubheda, Aja, Mūla, Varṇabhaṇṭha, Viḍaṅga, Jvālin, Mātṛrodana; (7) spoken by Kapālīśa, the Vāgīśa group: Bhairavī, Citrikā, Haṃsā, Kadambikā, Hṛllekhā, Candralekhā, Vidyullekhā, Vidyumān; (8) spoken by Unmatta, the Śikhā group: Bhairavī Śikhā, Vīṇā, Vīṇāmaṇi, Sammoha, Ḍāmara, Atharvaka, Kabandha, Śiraścheda. 'This is the wheel of Sadāśiva in eight groups of eight.'
speaker: Jayaratha (quoting the Śrīkaṇṭhīya)
notes: Phase-B author read the passage in the local e-text (sources_raw/raw_etexts/AgamAH/shaivam/tantrAlokaH_viveka-vyAkhyA-sahitaH-1.md (Tantrāloka with Jayaratha's Viveka, KSTS vol. 1)); level stays 'skeleton' until Phase C/D. Variant readings noted in the edition: Lampaṭādya, pañcālikā, Ajādya, Varṇāmaṭha, 'avardhaka'.

paraphrase: Jayaratha explains that the ten Śiva-divisions arise from the combinations of the Īśāna, Tatpuruṣa and Sadyojāta faces and are dominated by difference (bheda); the eighteen Rudra-divisions, from their combination with Vāmadeva and Aghora, are dominated by difference-and-non-difference; and the sixty-four Bhairava-divisions, when the other four faces are absorbed into the southern face, are dominated by non-duality. Thus scripture arose threefold — called Śiva, Rudra and Bhairava — because knowledge itself unfolds as difference, difference-and-non-difference and non-difference.
speaker: Jayaratha
notes: Phase-B author read the passage in the local e-text (sources_raw/raw_etexts/AgamAH/shaivam/tantrAlokaH_viveka-vyAkhyA-sahitaH-1.md (Tantrāloka with Jayaratha's Viveka, KSTS vol. 1)); level stays 'skeleton' until Phase C/D.

paraphrase: The Niśvāsamukha sets out a series of religious paths — worldly (laukika) religion, Vedic (vaidika) religion, the 'spiritual' (ādhyātmika) path of Sāṃkhya and Yoga, the Atimārga (Pāśupata and Lākula) and the Mantramārga — presenting them in ascending order.
notes: Chapter-level reference from memory of scholarship (N. Kafle's edition); exact chapters and verses not verified — the Niśvāsa is not in the local corpora. Compare the verified parallel at Kāmika pūrva 1.17–19.

paraphrase: Free from all pairs of opposites and devoid of all limiting adjuncts, the ṣāḍguṇya is the supreme Brahman, cause of all causes. Nārada asks what the ṣāḍguṇya is and how, if without qualities, it is called six-qualitied. Ahirbudhnya: it is called 'without qualities' with reference to the qualities of prakṛti, which do not touch it. Knowledge — non-inert, self-aware, eternal, all-penetrating — is the first quality, and it is both Brahman's nature and its quality; power (śakti) is its being the material cause of the world; lordship (aiśvarya) is its agency, full of independence; strength (bala) is its never tiring though ever making the world; virility (vīrya) is its undergoing no change though it is the material cause, also called 'not falling' (acyutatva); splendour (tejas) is its needing no auxiliary. These five are qualities of knowledge; knowledge alone is the supreme form of Brahman, the highest Self. That ṣāḍguṇya, the supreme Brahman, swelled by its own power, takes up the resolve 'may I be many' — that is Sudarśana.
speaker: Ahirbudhnya

original.text: सर्वद्वन्द्वविनिर्मुक्तं सर्वोपाधिविवर्जितम् । षाड्गुण्यं तत् परं ब्रह्म सर्वकारणकारणम् ॥ २-५३ ॥

notes: Phase-B author read the passage in the local e-text (sources_raw/raw_etexts/mixed/mukta/pAncharAtra/unknown/ahirbudhnya_saMhita_volume_1/2 (Adyar 1916 ed. as transcribed by Muktabodha)); level stays 'skeleton' until Phase C/D.

paraphrase: The pure creation proceeds from the six qualities by three pairs: from the pair of knowledge and strength arises Hari's form as Saṅkarṣaṇa; from the union of lordship and virility the form called Pradyumna; from the pre-eminence of power and splendour Aniruddha's body. These vyūhas, made of power, are marked by the manifestation of their qualities; yet they are embodiments of all six qualities, the remaining two pairs following along in each.
speaker: Ahirbudhnya
notes: Phase-B author read the passage in the local e-text (sources_raw/raw_etexts/mixed/mukta/pAncharAtra/unknown/ahirbudhnya_saMhita_volume_1/2 (Adyar 1916 ed. as transcribed by Muktabodha)); level stays 'skeleton' until Phase C/D.

paraphrase: The vibhavas are thirty-nine, beginning with Padmanābha: Padmanābha, Dhruva, Ananta, Śaktyātman, Madhusūdana, Vidyādhideva, Kapila, Viśvarūpa, Vihaṅgama, Kroḍātman, Baḍabāvaktra, Dharma, Vāgīśvara, the one lying on the single ocean, the Lord as tortoise, Varāha, Nārasiṃha, the nectar-taker, Śrīpati, Kāntātman, the nectar-bearer, the conqueror of Rāhu, the slayer of Kālanemi, the taker of the Pārijāta, Lokanātha, Śāntātman, Dattātreya, the one lying on the banyan, the one-horned, the dwarf, Trivikrama, Nara, Nārāyaṇa, Hari, Kṛṣṇa, Rāma with the blazing axe, Rāma with the bow, Vedavid, Kalkin and the one lying in Pātāla. Their origin, activity, weapons, forms, stations, ornaments, garments and powers are all told in the Sātvata teaching.
notes: Phase-B author read the passage in the local e-text (sources_raw/raw_etexts/mixed/mukta/pAncharAtra/unknown/ahirbudhnya_saMhita_volume_1/2 (Adyar 1916 ed. as transcribed by Muktabodha)); level stays 'skeleton' until Phase C/D. The segmentation of a few epithets into separate names is uncertain (the names can be counted as 39 or 40).

paraphrase: The Lord's resolve in the form of Sāṃkhya, uttered long ago by the sage Kapila, is the tantra called Sāṃkhya with sixty divisions in two circles. The natural (prākṛta) circle has thirty-two: the tantras of Brahman, of Puruṣa, three of Śakti, Niyati and Kāla, three of the guṇas, of the Imperishable, of Prāṇa, of the Agent, of the Master, five of the knowledge-senses, five of the action-organs, five of the subtle elements and five of the elements. The modified (vaikṛta) circle has twenty-eight sections: five on duties, and sections on experience, conduct, five afflictions, three means of knowledge, discernment (khyāti), dharma, detachment, lordship, the guṇas, the marks (liṅga), views, scriptural tradition, suffering, powers, the 'dyed' (kāṣāya), conventions (samaya) and liberation. This sixty-fold Sāṃkhya is made of Hari's Sudarśana.
speaker: Ahirbudhnya
notes: Phase-B author read the passage in the local e-text (sources_raw/raw_etexts/mixed/mukta/pAncharAtra/unknown/ahirbudhnya_saMhita_volume_1/2 (Adyar 1916 ed. as transcribed by Muktabodha)); level stays 'skeleton' until Phase C/D. Cross-reference for U09 (Sāṃkhya: the Ṣaṣṭitantra).

paraphrase: As the soul whirls in the wheel of transmigration by its own actions, afflicted by suffering, a certain compassion of Viṣṇu arises. That compassion is the fifth power already mentioned, of the form of Viṣṇu's will — the power of grace; those who hold to the āgamas call it Viṣṇu's descent of power (śaktipāta). When the soul is accepted by Viṣṇu with this power of grace, made of Sudarśana, a rain of compassion, and is looked upon by him, it attains equality of karmas (karmasāmya); that descent of power lifts the soul out of saṃsāra, the two karmas, being equal, falling silent — as robbers stop plundering and stand aside when the traveller has given up his belongings.
speaker: Ahirbudhnya
notes: Phase-B author read the passage in the local e-text (sources_raw/raw_etexts/mixed/mukta/pAncharAtra/unknown/ahirbudhnya_saMhita_volume_1/2 (Adyar 1916 ed. as transcribed by Muktabodha)); level stays 'skeleton' until Phase C/D.

paraphrase: Whatever desired thing is not attainable by other means — what the seeker of liberation cannot reach by Sāṃkhya, by yoga or by devotion — the supreme abode from which there is no return, and the supreme Self, Puruṣottama, are attained by surrender (nyāsa) alone. Knowers of the Veda say it is sixfold: the resolve to do what is agreeable, the avoidance of what is disagreeable, the faith that 'he will protect', the choosing (of him) as protector, the laying down of oneself, and helplessness — this is the sixfold refuge (śaraṇāgati). In this context the word 'śaraṇa', used for 'means' and for 'house' and 'protector', denotes the means alone.
speaker: Ahirbudhnya

original.text: आनुकूल्यस्य सङ्कल्पः प्रातिकूल्यस्य वर्जनम् । रक्षिष्यतीति विश्वासो गोप्तृत्ववरणं तथा ॥ आत्मनिक्षेपकार्पण्ये षड्विधा शरणागतिः ।

notes: Phase-B author read the passage in the local e-text (sources_raw/raw_etexts/mixed/mukta/pAncharAtra/unknown/ahirbudhnya_saMhita_volume_1/2 (Adyar 1916 ed. as transcribed by Muktabodha)); level stays 'skeleton' until Phase C/D.

paraphrase: Splendour (tejas) is called the sixth quality; some say it is the capacity to overcome others, others include it in lordship. These five qualities are pure outflowings of knowledge. These six qualities beginning with knowledge — the ṣāḍguṇya — are my body. From my wish to create there arises a minute part of me, by which the whole class of pure and impure is embraced; of these I shall explain the pure path, O lord of the gods.
speaker: Śrī (Lakṣmī)
notes: Phase-B author read the passage in the local e-text (sources_raw/raw_etexts/mixed/mukta/pAncharAtra/unknown/laxmItantra__M00206.md (Lakṣmī Tantra, Muktabodha e-text)); level stays 'skeleton' until Phase C/D.

paraphrase: I am Nārāyaṇa's power (śakti) — independent, the wondrous cause of all accomplishments, eternal, divine, ever arisen. Mine are five eternal acts, O lord of the gods: concealment (tirobhāva), creation, maintenance, dissolution and grace (anugraha) — this is called my fivefold work.
speaker: Śrī (Lakṣmī)
notes: Phase-B author read the passage in the local e-text (sources_raw/raw_etexts/mixed/mukta/pAncharAtra/unknown/laxmItantra__M00206.md (Lakṣmī Tantra, Muktabodha e-text)); level stays 'skeleton' until Phase C/D.

paraphrase: Means and non-means laid down in the śāstra were made by me: the prescribed are means, the prohibited non-means; non-means lead down one who follows them, means lead up. One who gives up both means and non-means, keeps to the middle course and takes refuge in me alone, reaches me in the end. Hear that six-limbed means: the resolve to do what is agreeable, the avoidance of the disagreeable, the faith that 'he will protect', choosing (him) as protector, laying down oneself, and helplessness — the sixfold refuge. Having thus taken refuge in me, free of grief, fear and weariness, without undertakings or desires, without 'mine' and without ego, one crosses the ocean of saṃsāra.

paraphrase: One who does not revile the scriptures and knows the higher and lower rules, a believer with faith, dear to Lakṣmī and her Lord, who knows the divisions of rite and sacrifice and the rules of other tantras, who knows yoga with its limbs and the truth of all śāstras, the Veda and its auxiliaries and the doctrine of Paśupati, who knows reasoning, the means of knowledge, logic and the categories, and the truth of all spiritual śāstras, is fit to receive (this teaching).

paraphrase: Nārāyaṇa himself is the speaker of the whole Pañcarātra. The Sātvata, the Pauṣkara and the Jayākhya are known as the three gems, issued directly from the Lord's mouth; the other tantras, also from his mouth, expand their essence by abridgement and expansion, as explanations do. Among the hundred and eight tantras, the Pārameśvara Saṃhitā explains the Pauṣkara, the Īśvara the Sātvata, and the Pādma the Jayākhya. Among the hundred and eight self-manifest places of the Lord four are chief — Śrīraṅgam, Veṅkaṭādri, Hastiśaila and Nārāyaṇādri; except at Veṅkaṭādri the three gems hold sway in the three others — the Sātvata at Yaduśaila, the Pauṣkara at Śrīraṅgam and the Jayākhya at Hastiśaila — while in practice the Pādma is followed at Hastiśaila, the Pārameśvara at Śrīraṅgam and the Īśvara at Yādavādri; of these Hastiśaila is pre-eminent.

original.text: सात्त्वतं पौष्करं चैव जयाख्यं तन्त्रमुत्तमम् । रत्नत्रयमिति ख्यातं तद्विशेष इहोच्यते ॥

notes: Phase-B author read the passage in the local e-text (sources_raw/raw_etexts/mixed/mukta/pAncharAtra/unknown/jayAkhyasaMhitA__M00123.md (Jayākhya Saṃhitā, Krishnamacharya's GOS ed. as transcribed)); level stays 'skeleton' until Phase C/D. The passage is marked as an additional reading in the edition; it is not part of the constituted text. It also explains the absence of Pāñcarātra at Veṅkaṭādri (Tirupati), a Vaikhānasa temple.

paraphrase: Thus the creation of Brahmā (brāhma sarga) has been told; many other gross creations of many forms have passed, beyond counting. Prior to it is the creation from primordial matter (prādhānika), and prior to that the highest, the Vaiṣṇava creation.
notes: Phase-B author read the passage in the local e-text (sources_raw/raw_etexts/mixed/mukta/pAncharAtra/unknown/jayAkhyasaMhitA__M00123.md (Jayākhya Saṃhitā, Krishnamacharya's GOS ed. as transcribed)); level stays 'skeleton' until Phase C/D. Paṭala 3 treats the prādhānika creation and paṭala 4 the pure creation ('śuddhasarga-brahmatattvākhyāna').

paraphrase: As the brahmin among the classes, the renouncer among the stages of life, the Gaṅgā among sacred fords and Acyuta among the gods, so the Pañcarātra is praised among all śāstras; whoever worships Hari by the Pañcarātra's rules attains supreme isolation (kaivalya), does not return to saṃsāra and gains imperishable fruit.
notes: Phase-B author read the passage in the local e-text (sources_raw/raw_etexts/mixed/ebhAratI-sampat/AgamaH/AgamasambaddhapustakAni/padmasaMhitA.md (jñānapāda)); level stays 'skeleton' until Phase C/D. A praise passage (cf. P7-arthavada).

paraphrase: The five other śāstras, however great, become like night (rātrīyante) in its presence; hence this name is current in the world. As the moon and stars do not shine by day, the five others do not shine near it; as nights come to an end when the sun blazes, so do the others before it. This śāstra is holy, destroying sin and becoming, a great ship carrying across the ocean of existence those sunk in it and bound by the noose of karma.
notes: Phase-B author read the passage in the local e-text (sources_raw/raw_etexts/mixed/ebhAratI-sampat/AgamaH/AgamasambaddhapustakAni/padmasaMhitA.md (jñānapāda)); level stays 'skeleton' until Phase C/D. The Pādma's own etymology of the name; the 'five other śāstras' are not named in these verses.

paraphrase: As the Veda is divided fourfold as Ṛg and the rest, so the Pañcarātra is fourfold by siddhānta, and as each Veda divides into many branches, each siddhānta divides by its speakers. It is called 'siddhānta' because those who have reached settled conclusions in Mīmāṃsā and the other śāstras become eligible for it at the end. That in which one form predominates is the Mantra-siddhānta; that in which four forms predominate is the Āgama-siddhānta; that in which nine forms predominate is the Tantra-siddhānta; that in which worship is of a god with four or three faces is the Tantrāntara. (V. 83 names Vāsudeva and the other three, and Nārāyaṇa, Hayagrīva, Viṣṇu, Nṛhari and the Boar.)
notes: Phase-B author read the passage in the local e-text (sources_raw/raw_etexts/mixed/ebhAratI-sampat/AgamaH/AgamasambaddhapustakAni/padmasaMhitA.md (jñānapāda)); level stays 'skeleton' until Phase C/D.

paraphrase: The objector holds that the Pāñcarātra is not a valid means of knowledge: its validity cannot rest on perception, inference or the Veda; its followers, the Sātvatas or Bhāgavatas, are not brahmins but a class who serve in temples for a living, as smṛti texts describe (e.g. the Sātvata listed among the offspring of degraded twice-born); smṛti verses class the Pāñcarātra with Śaiva, Pāśupata, Buddhist, Jain and Kāpāla doctrines as outside the Veda; and Bādarāyaṇa refutes it in the Brahma Sūtra.
notes: The anti-Pāñcarātra position as presented by its opponent Yāmuna. Phase-B author read the passage in the local e-text (sources_raw/raw_etexts/mixed/mukta/pAncharAtra/yAmunAchArya/AgamaprAmANya__M00001.md (ed. Rāmamiśra Śāstrī, Benares 1937)); level stays 'skeleton' until Phase C/D. The work has no numbered sections; refs are by argument-section.

paraphrase: Yāmuna answers that the Pāñcarātra is valid because it was spoken by the omniscient Lord Vāsudeva; its followers are brahmins, called Sātvata or Bhāgavata because of a quality, as brahmins are called 'renouncers'; the verses condemning outside doctrines concern the Kāpālika, Kālāmukha, Pāśupata and Śaiva schools and the like, not the Bhagavat's scripture; and Vyāsa (Bādarāyaṇa), himself a supreme Bhāgavata, cannot be imagined to refute the Bhāgavata teaching — the sūtras on the origination of the soul are rightly understood as not refuting it.
notes: Phase-B author read the passage in the local e-text (sources_raw/raw_etexts/mixed/mukta/pAncharAtra/yAmunAchArya/AgamaprAmANya__M00001.md (ed. Rāmamiśra Śāstrī, Benares 1937)); level stays 'skeleton' until Phase C/D. The Ekāyana-śruti argument for the Pāñcarātra's Vedic root was not found in this e-text (it appears in Vedānta Deśika's Pāñcarātrarakṣā).

paraphrase: Four sūtras: (42) because origination is impossible; (43) and (because) the instrument (does not arise) from the agent; (44) or, if (they) are of the nature of knowledge and the rest, there is no denial of that; (45) and because of contradiction.
speaker: Bādarāyaṇa

differs_from.note: Śaṅkara reads all four as refuting the Bhāgavata doctrine
Rāmānuja reads 44–45 as answering the objection in 42–43

notes: The sūtras do not name their target; the Bhāgavata/Pāñcarātra reference is supplied by the commentators. Contribution from U08; U13 owns the Brahma Sūtra.

paraphrase: Śaṅkara reports the Bhāgavata teaching: Vāsudeva, the highest Self, abides divided fourfold as Vāsudeva, Saṅkarṣaṇa (the individual soul), Pradyumna (mind) and Aniruddha (ego-sense), and is to be approached by going to the temple, gathering materials, worship, study and yoga. He accepts the worship and meditation of Vāsudeva as not contrary to scripture, but rejects the origination of the soul (Saṅkarṣaṇa) from Vāsudeva, since an originated soul would be impermanent and could not attain liberation; he also finds contradiction and opposition to the Veda in the system, citing its account that Śāṇḍilya learned this śāstra after not finding the highest good in the four Vedas.
speaker: Śaṅkara
notes: The Pāñcarātra doctrine here is reported by its critic. Paraphrase from memory; not checked against a local e-text. The five practices named correspond to the Pāñcarātra's five daily periods.

paraphrase: Rāmānuja takes the first two sūtras as stating the objection that the Pāñcarātra teaches the origination of the soul, and the last two as its answer: since Saṅkarṣaṇa and the others are the highest Brahman itself in its forms, possessed of knowledge and the other qualities, the objection does not touch them, and the Pāñcarātra itself denies the origination of the soul; so its authority stands.
speaker: Rāmānuja
notes: Paraphrase from memory; not checked against a local e-text. Contribution from U08; U14 owns the Śrībhāṣya.

paraphrase: By the same reasoning that sets aside smṛti in conflict with the Veda, Kumārila rejects the teachings on dharma and adharma accepted by the Sāṃkhya, Yoga, Pāñcarātra, Pāśupata, Buddhists and Jains, as not grounded in the Veda.
speaker: Kumārila
notes: Location recalled as the Tantravārttika on MS 1.3.4; wording and exact place not verified. U12 owns the Tantravārttika.

paraphrase: Puruṣa Nārāyaṇa desired: 'May I surpass all beings; may I alone be this whole world.' He saw this five-day (pañcarātra) sacrificial rite, the Puruṣamedha, took it and sacrificed with it, and so surpassed all beings and became this whole world.

paraphrase: After worshipping the fixed image (dhruva) with eight services by mantra, one should perform worship with thirty-two services in the kautuka image. The supreme Brahman, Nārāyaṇa, is called the highest Self; its highest form is subtle, imperishable and partless (niṣkala), and the fixed image stands in its place; since partless worship is impossible, worship of the fixed image is only the placing of flowers. Viṣṇu's form with parts (sakala), gross and the cause of all, is represented by the kautuka image, and there worship is to be done, because offerings of flowers and the like can be made to it; worship is prescribed where there is a support and parts, while the fixed image, being partless, is without support.

paraphrase: Ten reasons are set out why the Vaikhānasa Sūtra — composed by the four-faced Brahmā called Vikhanas, born of Nārāyaṇa, the supreme Brahman possessing truth and all auspicious qualities — is the best of all sūtras, and those who follow its dharma the most excellent of all: because it was composed by Vikhanas, the cause of the whole world; because it is the first of all sūtras; because in all rites it follows the path of the śruti; because it teaches all rites with mantras; because it has the rite of impregnation and the other saṃskāras; because it teaches the eighteen bodily saṃskāras; because it has the full set of rites with their subsidiaries; and further reasons — each established from śruti, smṛti and purāṇa.
speaker: Śrīnivāsa Dīkṣita

paraphrase: Is Vikhanas some sage, or Nārāyaṇa? Nārāyaṇa alone: no mere sage is taught to be denoted by 'Vaikhānasa', whereas śruti, smṛti and purāṇa show that the supreme Self Nārāyaṇa is denoted by 'Vikhanas', 'Vaikhānasa' and the like — as in the khila-śruti: 'the cow (is the source) of draught animals, Aditi of the gods, Brahmā of the Ṛbhus, Vikhanas of the sages'.

paraphrase: The Goddess says to Bhairava: you have revealed to me all mantras and the sixty-four tantras of the Mothers, the best — Mahāmāyā, Śambara, Yoginījālaśambara, Tattvaśambara, the eight Bhairava tantras, the eight Bahurūpas, the eight Yāmalas, Candrajñāna, Vāsuki, Mahāsammohana, Mahocchuṣma, Vātula, Vātulottara, Hṛdbheda, Tantrabheda, Guhyatantra, Kāmika, Kalāvāda, Kalāsāra, Kubjikāmata, Tantrottara, Vīṇākhya, Trotala, Trotalottara, Pañcāmṛta, Rūpabheda, Bhūtoḍḍāmara, Kulasāra, Kuloḍḍīśa, Kulacūḍāmaṇi, Sarvajñānottara, Mahākālīmata, Mahālakṣmīmata, Siddhayogeśvarīmata, Kurūpikāmata, Devarūpikāmata, Sarvavīramata, Vimalāmata, the Eastern, Western, Southern, Northern and Niruttara, Vaiśeṣika, Jñāna, Vīrāvali, Aruṇeśa, Mohinīśa and Viśuddheśvara — these and crores of other śāstras, all made of knowledge, have been told by you.
speaker: the Goddess
notes: Phase-B author read the passage in the local e-text (sources_raw/raw_etexts/mixed/ebhAratI-sampat/AgamaH/tantrashAstram/nityAShoDashikArNavaH.md (Nityāṣoḍaśikārṇava with Bhāskararāya's Setubandha)); level stays 'skeleton' until Phase C/D. Bhāskararāya's Setubandha glosses the eight Bhairavas as Asitāṅga, Ruru, Caṇḍa, Krodha, Unmatta, Kapālin, Bhīṣaṇa, Saṃhāra (noting other lists), the Bahurūpas as the tantras of the seven Mothers and Śivadūtī, discusses how the count of 64 is reached (e.g. 'mahādeva' as a vocative), and takes the Vāmakeśvara itself as the independent 65th tantra of Saundaryalaharī 31 (Gaurīkānta: the Jñānārṇava). paraphrase: Paśupati beguiled the whole world with sixty-four tantras, each bent on producing its own particular powers, and rested; then, at your insistence, he brought down to earth this tantra of yours, which by itself brings about all the aims of human life.

paraphrase: Lakṣmīdhara characterises the sixty-four tantras one by one (many as Kāpālika, left-handed or aimed at worldly powers) and concludes that they deceive even those who know them, being aimed only at powers in this world and far from the Vedic path. Paśupati made tantras for different classes: the sixty-four are for śūdras and mixed classes; the three higher classes are eligible for the eight Candrakalā tantras (Candrakalā, Jyotsnāvatī, Kalānidhi, Kulārṇava, Kuleśvarī, Bhuvaneśvarī, Bārhaspatya, Durvāsamata), which teach the right-hand way for them and the left-hand way for others and are called 'mixed'. The five auspicious āgamas — the saṃhitās of Vasiṣṭha, Sanaka, Śuka, Sanandana and Sanatkumāra — teach the Vedic way, called Samayācāra, which his commentary follows; 'the mixed and the Kaula paths are to be abandoned'.
speaker: Lakṣmīdhara
